newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FOCUS-Australia crudes see 9-day lifting delays.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Australia crudes see 9-day lifting delays.

text.p: The closure of Australia's Cossack and Griffin crude fields in recent weeks has prompted a nine-day delay in liftings, industry sources said on Friday.
Some refiners on the east coast have been forced to put back production schedules by a bout a week because of the delay in lifting crudes from the northwestern oil fields, they said.

And others are finding it difficult to secure tankers for fill-in crude deliveries to their refineries in Australia because of a generally tight Afromax (80,000 deadweight tonnes) market, the trade and shipping sources said.
The cyclones have left several tankers waiting to load Cossack and Griffin. Shipping sources said the delays were around nine days.
However, they said there were no delays to loadings at Barrow Island or Thevenard.
But some refiners were enquiring about replacement barrels so that they could maintain refinery output schedules.

One producer brought forward term supplies of Alaskan North Slope (ANS), its normal feedstock crude, for its Hawaii refinery to fill in the slot that had been allotted for processing the lighter Griffin crude.
The 90,000 barrels per day offshore Cossack field aimed to restart production on Friday in the wake of Cyclone Rachel on Friday, operator Woodside Petroleum Ltd said.
Broken Hill Pty Ltd, the operator of the 70,000 bpd Griffin field, said it was monitoring sea conditions to determine when to reconnect the floating production vessel.
The fields have been shut down for most of the past two weeks, first owing to Cyclone Phil and then Rachel.
The 15,000-bpd Barrow Island, 30,000 bpd Thevenard and 30,000 bpd Challis fields were also affected by the cyclone -- but to a lesser extent, crude traders said.
But for Australian based refiners, potential replacement crudes like Gippsland and Kutubu appear tight, the sources said.
There were no Gippsland spot availabilities until after the first quarter of 1997 and possibly not until even later.
There were few spot availabilities of Kutubu until March liftings, traders said. Two February cargoes, owned by two majors, were likely to be held in house, traders said.
But shipping brokers and charterers said that even if spot crude were available, the shipping market was extremely tight.

One U.S. major was seeking to charter a tanker between the Middle East and its refinery in Australia as far forward as February 2 because of the tightness of the nearby market. Few offers had emerged.

And another U.S. major had secured an Afromax class tanker for Indonesia to the Australian east coast for January 23-25 in a move to seek fill-in barrels because of the delay in liftings at Cossack and Griffin.
"Most players have just got to weather the delays," one shipper said. "They will eventually need the crude in any event, so they might as well lift it."
Afromax shipping rates were valued worldscale 130-140, with an end January recently fixed at W137.5.
However, brokers said at the moment there was no great pressure on rates because availability was extremely tight anyway and the market was returning to work after New Year.
And many of the refiners have shared or their own tanker tonnage to use.
"But the pressure could be up there in the next few weeks if anyone is caught with a spot position. Then there will be some pain," one charterer said. "It could hit WS140 quite easily."
--Singapore Newsroom (+65 870 3081)
